tier_reason: docs/OverallComparison.md is BenchmarkDotNet output from benchmarks/Quickenshtein.Benchmarks/Comparisons/QuickComparisonBenchmark.cs (public), comparing the repo's naive LevenshteinBaseline.cs and Fastenshtein, with .NET Core SDK 5.0.201 / .NET Core 5.0.4 RyuJIT and .NET Framework 4.8, BenchmarkDotNet ShortRun job and Intel Core i7-6700HQ stated, so code, toolchain, job settings and CPU model are all present.

corrections.claimed_speedup: docs/OverallComparison.md (BenchmarkDotNet, i7-6700HQ), 8000 characters on .NET Core 5.0: Baseline 356,315,300.0 ns, Quickenshtein 17,253,112.5 ns, Quickenshtein_Threaded 16,973,617.7 ns, Fastenshtein 82,207,344.4 ns. The table's 20.92x Speedup column is relative to the .NET 4.7.2 Baseline job (360,927,200.0 ns); against the same-runtime .NET Core 5.0 Baseline it is about 20.65x (derived from page data), and Quickenshtein is about 4.76x faster than Fastenshtein (derived from page data). 400 characters on .NET Core 5.0: Quickenshtein 64,781.7 ns vs Fastenshtein 342,278.1 ns, about 5.28x (derived from page data). 10 characters on .NET Core 5.0: Quickenshtein 317.7 ns vs Fastenshtein 181.4 ns (slower). docs/IntrinsicsPerformance.md (8000-character run): all intrinsics 17.31 ms, without AVX2 (COMPlus_EnableAVX2=0) 28.94 ms, no intrinsics (COMPlus_EnableHWIntrinsic=0) 100.04 ms, so the SIMD path is about 5.78x faster than the library's own scalar path (derived from page data).
corrections.caveats: Slower than Fastenshtein on 10-character strings on .NET Core 5.0 (317.7 ns vs 181.4 ns). On .NET Framework 4.7.2 (no hardware intrinsics) Quickenshtein loses to Fastenshtein at 400 characters (625,731.9 ns vs 346,120.9 ns) and ties it at 8000 characters single-threaded (99,787,886.7 ns vs 101,566,466.7 ns); it wins there only in threaded mode (30,820,936.5 ns), which compares multi-threaded against single-threaded Fastenshtein. The 'Baseline' is a deliberately naive jagged-matrix implementation built with LINQ that allocates the full (n+1)x(m+1) matrix (256 MB at 8000 characters), so the 20x figure is against a strawman; Fastenshtein (about 4.8x) and the library's own no-intrinsics path (about 5.8x) are the meaningful comparisons. The table's Ratio/Speedup columns are relative to the .NET 4.7.2 Baseline job, not the same-runtime baseline. ShortRun job with 3 iterations and 1 launch, so error bars are wide (Quickenshtein 8000 chars: error 3,559,513.67 ns). One synthetic string pair built by repeating 'aabcdecbaabcadbab' and 'babdacbaabcedcbaa'. Published numbers come from an older revision (.NET Core 5.0, BenchmarkDotNet 0.12.1); the current benchmark project targets net6.0 and net472 with BenchmarkDotNet 0.13.4 and Fastenshtein 1.0.0.8, so HEAD reproduces a different configuration. C# library, not C++.

notes: Numbers match OverallComparison.md and IntrinsicsPerformance.md exactly; the only claim fix is that the 20.92x column is relative to the .NET 4.7.2 Baseline job (20.65x vs the same-runtime baseline, derived). Main shortcomings for decisions.json: strawman baseline (naive LINQ jagged-matrix), slower than Fastenshtein on 10-char strings and on .NET Framework at 400 chars, stale docs from .NET 5, C# not C++; category simd-intrinsics-libraries fits loosely (it is a Levenshtein library that uses SIMD, closer to a string-algorithms category). Last commit 2023-08-01 (dependency bump), more than 3 years old, so 'abandoned' stands; license MIT (License.txt), 315 stars.

tier_reason: README Performance section compares each SIMD kernel with its pure-Go scalar reference using public benchmarks (f64/benchmark_test.go and the other packages' benchmark tests, run via Taskfile.yml 'task bench' = go test -bench=. -benchmem), and states the Go 1.26 toolchain, performance governor, best-of-repeated-runs protocol and CPU models (Intel Core i7-1260P, Raspberry Pi 5 Cortex-A76).

corrections.caveats: Baseline is the library's own pure-Go loop, and the README notes Go 1.26 generates tighter scalar loops than older toolchains, shrinking elementwise gains. The reduction references are single-accumulator serial loops (f64/f64_go.go: dotProductGo chains math.FMA into one sum even though unrolled by 4; sumGo is a plain 'sum += v' loop), so they are latency-bound and part of the 12-16x reduction speedups comes from breaking that dependency chain, which a multi-accumulator scalar loop would also get; Go's compiler does not auto-vectorize. The 73x Tanh and 19x Exp figures compare a fast approximation (max relative error about 7e-6 for f32) with the exact math.Tanh and math.Exp. The float32 table mixes runs (Variance/StdDev re-measured after fix #214 under a median-of-9 protocol, other rows from one earlier run) and its Variance/StdDev Go figures come from SIMD_DISABLE=all because those benchmarks have no Go sub-benchmark. Exact Go patch version not stated. Hardware is two consumer machines; comparisons shown are against the pure-Go path only, not another Go SIMD library or a C/C++ SIMD library.

notes: All quoted figures appear in README Performance (DotProduct 54 vs 887 ns 16.5x, EuclideanDistance 15.4x, Mean 12.7x, Sum 12.1x, Clamp 10.6x, Add 2.4x, Div 2.0x, CumulativeSum 1.0x, NEON f32 3.5-5.2x and f64 2.4-2.6x, Tanh 73x, Exp 19x) and in Performance Notes. Shortcomings: self-written scalar baseline with single-accumulator reductions, approximation-vs-exact activation rows, Go not C++, 26 stars. Metadata verified: MIT, last commit 2026-10-05, active, not a fork.

tier_reason: README shows first-party go test -bench output from hash_test.go (public) against minio/sha256-simd, but no Go version is given with the numbers and the CPU models are missing (x86 shown only as 'Intel(R) Xeon(R) CPU @ 2.80GHz', an unnamed darwin/arm64 machine and an unnamed Raspberry Pi), so it falls short of A.

corrections.baseline: minio/sha256-simd v1.0.0 via sha256.New() (one 64-byte message per call); on CPUs without SHA extensions this New() falls back to Go's standard crypto/sha256.New(), so the Xeon and Raspberry Pi rows effectively ran Go stdlib crypto/sha256
corrections.caveats: The minio baseline is minio/sha256-simd v1.0.0 (go.mod), whose New() returns Go's crypto/sha256.New() when the CPU lacks SHA extensions (sha256.go, New): its AVX-512 multi-buffer code is only reachable through the separate Avx512Server API, so the record's 'AVX-512' description of the baseline does not apply. On the Xeon (Hash_1 473.1 ns for one 64-byte message, consistent with no SHA-NI) and the Raspberry Pi without crypto extensions, the baseline therefore effectively ran Go stdlib crypto/sha256 single-buffer; only the Apple arm64 row used minio's own ARM SHA2 path. The gain is multi-buffer (many independent 64-byte blocks per call) versus one message per call. The baseline benchmarks also pay a sha256.New() allocation and hash.Hash interface calls per message, and BenchmarkHashLargeList_minio allocates a 64-byte slice per pair through append and hashes 199,999 pairs (loop starts at j=1) versus 200,000 for BenchmarkHashList. Special-purpose (pairs of 32-byte chunks, Merkle layers), not a general SHA-256 replacement. CPU models and Go version missing. It is the Go-assembly port of prysmaticlabs/hashtree (now OffchainLabs/hashtree, already verified in wave 7, crypto-hashes).

notes: Numbers all match the README (Xeon Hash_16 7933 vs 1988 ns, LargeList 105,404,666 vs 25,368,532 ns; darwin arm64 Hash_16 1974 vs 689.2 ns; Raspberry Pi Hash_16 67142 vs 13351 ns; Xeon Hash_1 473.1 vs 391.3 ns), and derived ratios are correct. Consider decision 'duplicate': the README calls it the Go Assembly counterpart of hashtree, and https://github.com/offchainlabs/hashtree is verified in wave 7 (its record already names gohashtree as Prysm's Go-assembly port); go-quickjs/goant port precedent. Category simd-intrinsics-libraries fits loosely (hand-written Go assembly SHA-256; crypto-hashes or hand-written-asm-kernels is closer).
